questions.prompt: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language.
questions.explain: Yes - HTML is a markup language. It describes the structure and meaning of content with tags; it does not compute anything.

questions.prompt: Which tag creates the largest heading on a page?
questions.explain: <h1> is the biggest heading and should be used once per page. Headings count DOWN: <h2>, <h3> ... <h6> is the smallest.

questions.prompt: Which tag wraps a paragraph of text?

is one block of text.

questions.prompt: Which attribute gives an image a text alternative for screen readers?
questions.explain: alt holds the alternative text. If the image cannot load, or a screen reader is used, alt is what the user receives.

questions.prompt: Which line creates a link the user can click?
questions.explain: The anchor tag <a> plus the href attribute makes a hyperlink. <link> is different - it attaches resources such as stylesheets and renders nothing.

questions.prompt: What does this markup look like in the browser?
questions.explain: <ul> is an unordered list, so items get bullets. An ordered list uses <ol>, which numbers them 1, 2, 3.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a void element - one that has no closing tag?
questions.explain: is a void element: it never wraps content, so it needs no . The other three all wrap content and must be closed.

questions.prompt: Where must the <title> element live?
questions.explain: <head> holds metadata - the title, character set, stylesheets. Only what the user actually sees goes in <body>.

questions.prompt: CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets.
questions.explain: Correct. "Cascading" means several rules can target the same element, and the browser resolves which one wins by specificity and source order.

questions.prompt: Which property changes the colour of text?
questions.explain: The property is simply `color`. `background-color` paints the box behind the text - a very common mix-up for beginners.

questions.prompt: Which selector targets only elements with class="bata"?
questions.explain:
A dot selects a class. A hash selects an id, and a bare word selects a tag name such as

.

questions.prompt: What does this rule change?
choices: The size of the text inside every <h2>
The thickness of the heading border
questions.explain: font-size sets how tall the glyphs are. Box width is `width`, and spacing is `margin` or `padding`.

questions.prompt: Which unit is relative to the root font size, so it scales with the user settings?
questions.explain: 1rem equals the root font size. rem scaling respects accessibility settings, while px is a fixed pixel and never scales.

questions.prompt: Which property adds space INSIDE an element, between its content and its border?
questions.explain: Padding is inside the border. Margin is outside it, pushing other elements away. The box model reads: content -> padding -> border -> margin.

questions.prompt: Both rules target the same paragraph. Which declaration wins?
choices: color: red - an id is more specific than a class
color: blue - classes are read after ids
Neither, the browser picks at random
questions.explain: Specificity: id (100) beats class (10) beats tag (1). Only when specificity is tied does the later rule win - here the id always wins.

questions.prompt: Which value hides an element but still reserves its space in the layout?
questions.explain: visibility: hidden keeps the box in place (invisible but still occupying its slot). display: none removes the box entirely, so the layout collapses.

questions.prompt: Which keyword declares a variable that cannot be reassigned?
questions.explain: const creates a block-scoped binding that cannot be reassigned. let is the same but reassignable. Prefer const until the value truly must change.

questions.prompt: In JavaScript a single equals sign ( = ) compares two values for equality.
questions.explain: False. A single = assigns a value. To compare, use === (strict, no type conversion) or == (loose, converts types first). Prefer ===.

questions.prompt: What does this line do?
questions.explain: console.log() writes its argument to the browser console (F12, then Console). It is the beginner best friend for checking what a value really is.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explain: The right-hand side is evaluated first: n + 3 is 8, then the result is stored back into n. Printing n gives 8.

questions.prompt: What is the value of typeof "7" ?
questions.explain: Quotes make it text, so typeof reports "string". Remember "7" (string) is not 7 (number) - a classic bug when reading form input.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: With a string operand, + concatenates: JavaScript converts the number 2 to text and joins them, giving "22". Use Number("2") + 2 for arithmetic.

questions.prompt: What does this loop print, in order?
questions.explain: i starts at 0 and runs while i < 3, so the body sees 0, 1, 2. The loop stops the moment i becomes 3, so 3 is never printed.

questions.prompt: Which expression gives the number of items in the array?
questions.explain: Arrays expose `length` as a property (no parentheses). Functions use parentheses, properties do not - that difference trips up almost every beginner.

questions.prompt: Which keyword starts a function definition in Python?
questions.explain: Python uses `def`. Note the colon at the end of the line and the indented body - both are required.

questions.prompt: Python uses indentation to define code blocks instead of curly braces.
questions.explain: True. In Python the whitespace IS the syntax. A block that is not indented consistently raises an IndentationError.

questions.prompt: Which line prints the word Kalinga?
questions.explain: print() is the Python 3 output function. echo is shell/PHP, console.log is JavaScript, and printf is C.

questions.prompt: What is the value of the expression 7 // 2 ?
questions.explain: The // operator is floor division: it divides and rounds down to the whole number 3. A single / gives 3.5, and % gives the remainder 1.

questions.prompt: What does len([10, 20, 30]) return?
questions.explain: len() counts the items in a sequence: three elements gives 3. It does not add them up.

questions.prompt: Which of these creates a dictionary (key to value) rather than a list?
questions.explain: Curly braces with key: value pairs make a dict. Square brackets make a list, parentheses a tuple, and braces holding only values a set.

questions.prompt: Which numbers does this loop print?
questions.explain: range(3) produces 0, 1, 2 - it stops BEFORE the stop value. range(1, 4) would give 1, 2, 3.

questions.prompt: What is type(3.5) in Python?
questions.explain: A number with a decimal point is a float in Python. int has no decimal point, and `double` is a C/Java name - Python only has float.

questions.prompt: Which method signature is the entry point Java runs first?
questions.explain: Java looks for exactly `public static void main(String[] args)`. Change the name, the static modifier or the return type and the program will not start.

questions.prompt: Java is case-sensitive, so `String` and `string` are different names.
questions.explain: True. `String` with a capital S compiles because it is a class; `string` does not exist. Java is strict about capitalisation everywhere.

questions.prompt: Which keyword creates a new object from a class?
questions.explain: `new` allocates the object and calls a constructor. Java has no `create` or `make` keyword.

questions.prompt: Which type stores a whole number such as 42?
questions.explain: int holds a 32-bit whole number. String is text, boolean is true/false, and char holds a single character in single quotes.

questions.prompt: What does this line print?
choices: An error, quotes are not allowed
questions.explain: println prints the text and then moves to a new line. The quotes are delimiters and are not printed - the console shows just Hi.

questions.prompt: Which keyword marks a variable as a constant that cannot change later?
questions.explain: In Java the modifier is `final`. C++ and JavaScript use `const` instead - that is the mix-up to remember.

questions.prompt: What is stored in x?
questions.explain: Both operands are int, so Java performs INTEGER division and throws the remainder away, giving 2. Write 5 / 2.0 if you need 2.5.

questions.prompt: Which line correctly declares a String variable?
questions.explain: Capital S for the String class, then the name, then a double-quoted literal, then a semicolon. Single quotes are only for the char type.

questions.prompt: Which header must be included to use std::cout?
questions.explain: <iostream> is the input/output stream header that defines std::cout and std::cin. <stdio.h> is the older C library (printf) and provides no cout.

questions.prompt: Which operator sends data INTO std::cout?
questions.explain: The insertion operator << points INTO the output stream. >> points into a variable (used with cin). The arrow direction shows which way data flows.

questions.prompt: C++ statements must end with a semicolon.
questions.explain: True. A missing semicolon is the most common first compiler error, and the message usually points at the line AFTER the real mistake.

questions.prompt: Which type stores a true/false value?
questions.explain: The C++ type is `bool`, short for boolean. It is not spelled `boolean` - that spelling belongs to Java.

questions.prompt: What is the value of a after these lines?
questions.explain: The ++ operator increments by 1, so a becomes 11. (a-- would have made it 9.)

questions.prompt: Which function does a C++ program start executing from?
questions.explain: Execution always begins at main(). It returns an int to the operating system, where 0 means "finished successfully".

questions.prompt: What does the std:: prefix in std::cout mean?
choices: cout lives in the standard namespace
questions.explain: std is the standard-library namespace and :: is the scope-resolution operator. `using namespace std;` lets you drop the prefix, at the cost of clearer code.

questions.prompt: What is stored in x?
questions.explain: Both operands are int, so this is integer division and the result is 2. Write 5 / 2.0 or use a double to keep the fractional part.
